claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Deregulated genes in geriatric samples were enriched for glutathione metabolic process [GO:0006749] and genes in the drug metabolism -cytochrome P450 pathway.
claims.source: Deregulated genes in geriatric samples were enriched for glutathione metabolic process [GO:0006749] as well as genes in the drug metabolism -cytochrome P450 pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: An upregulation of neuronal genes that are also markers of EE cells such as Sytalpha, nrv3 and dysc was observed in both old and geriatric samples.
claims.source: We also noticed an upregulation of neuronal genes that are also markers of EE cells such as Sytalpha, nrv3 and dysc in both old and geriatric samples (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) with gene sets of EE or EC-specific genes revealed a consistent and significant enrichment of EE genes in the genes upregulated in aging ISCs.
claims.source: Accordingly, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) with gene sets of 58 or 51 previously described EE or EC-specific genes, respectively (Dutta et al., 2015), revealed a consistent and significant enrichment of EE genes in the genes upregulated in aging ISCs (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: EC genes were downregulated at the old time-point.
claims.source: EC genes were downregulated at the old time-point, and no significant trends were observed for these genes in other comparisons (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: scRNA-seq was performed on whole midguts at young, mid-age, and old time-points.
claims.source: We performed scRNA-seq on whole midguts at young, mid-age, and old time-points and a total of 4880 young, 1440 mid-aged, and 5829 old cells were used in our final analyses.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Clustering analysis revealed nine clusters that could be classified into the major cell types and sub-cell types of the midgut.
claims.source: After batch correction, clustering analysis revealed nine clusters that could be classified into the major cell types and sub-cell types of the midgut that have been recently described (Hung et al., 2020; Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq clustering analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: An age-associated increase in mitotically active ISCs was confirmed by scRNA-seq.
claims.source: Focusing on age-related changes in the ISC/EB populations, we confirmed the well-characterized (Jasper, 2020) age-associated increase in mitotically active ISCs, which separated into a distinct cluster (#3) that consisted of cells with elevated expression of cell cycle and mitotic genes (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Two cell clusters (#4 and 8) were almost exclusively present in samples from old flies.
claims.source: Two cell clusters (#4 and 8) were almost exclusively present in samples from old flies (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The transcriptomes of cells from clusters #4 and #8 were enriched for transcripts encoding genes involved in DNA repair, TNFalpha/NFkB signaling and protein secretion.
claims.source: The transcriptomes of cells from these clusters were enriched for transcripts encoding genes involved in DNA repair, TNFalpha/NFkB signaling and protein secretion, while transcripts involved in the cell cycle and mitosis were depleted or downregulated compared to other clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: A significant correlation of differentially expressed genes was observed when comparing young with mid-aged and young with old samples in pseudo bulk analysis.
claims.source: We observed a significant correlation of differentially expressed genes when comparing young with mid-aged and young with old samples (correlation is weaker in the second comparison, potentially due to an age-related increase of transcriptional noise, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pseudo bulk analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Age-associated genetic changes in Clusters 1–3 showed the most significant enrichment and gene expression overlap with bulk RNA-seq gene sets.
claims.source: We also found that age-associated genetic changes in Clusters 1–3 showed the most significant enrichment and gene expression overlap with our bulk RNA-seq gene sets (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pseudo bulk analysis and GSEA shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Cluster #4 consists of stressed cells.
claims.source: GO analysis on gene module 12 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) revealed enrichment of stress-associated terms such as 'glutathione metabolic process', 'chaperone-mediated protein folding' and 'response to heat' (Figure 2C), suggesting that Cluster #4 consists of stressed cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Many significantly upregulated genes from the bulk RNA-seq were also upregulated in Cluster #4.
claims.source: Of note, we found that many significantly upregulated genes from the bulk RNA-seq were also upregulated in Cluster #4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 4), suggesting that the most pronounced expression changes observed in bulk ISCs reflect the acquisition of the 'aged/stressed ISC' state.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Cluster #8 consists of damaged cells.
claims.source: Module 18 genes are upregulated in Cluster #8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B) and show enrichment for DNA repair, DNA damage and telomere stress induced senescence pathways (Figure 2C), indicating damaged cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The appearance of 'stressed' or damaged cell states in old intestines is consistent with reported elevated stress signaling as well as DNA damage in the aged epithelium.
claims.source: The appearance of these 'stressed' or damaged cell states in old intestines is consistent with reported elevated stress signaling as well as DNA damage in the aged epithelium (Buchon et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014; Hochmuth et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012; Siudeja et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Loss of activity of the antioxidant response regulator, CncC/Nrf2, leads to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in old ISCs during aging.
claims.source: During aging, loss of activity of the antioxidant response regulator, CncC/Nrf2, leads to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in old ISCs (Hochmuth et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: High levels of ROS have been linked to increased DNA damage in ISCs.
claims.source: High levels of ROS have been linked to increased DNA damage in these cells, an observation that is supported by our results (Park et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and by the scRNA-seq data showing DNA damage signatures.

claims.claim: Gene expression trajectory analysis for Cluster #5 revealed the progression of EE differentiation from EE-specified (Pros+/esg+) ISC progenitors to mature EEs.
claims.source: To explore possible changes in lineage specification further, we performed gene expression trajectory analysis for Cluster #5 as it consists of EE progenitor cells. This revealed the progression of EE differentiation from EE-specified (Pros+/esg+) ISC progenitors to mature EEs, and included mitotic EE progenitors, which most likely represent a mitotic phase during EE specification that has recently been described (Chen et al., 2018; He et al., 2018; Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: A significant increase in the number of EE progenitor cells in old samples was observed.
claims.source: Focusing on the EE progenitor sub-cluster (based on Delta (Dl) and asense (ase) expression and lack of nervana 3 (nrv3), a mature EE marker), we observed a significant increase in the number of EE progenitor cells in old samples (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Old EE progenitors had increased expression of deadpan (dpn) and other pro-neural genes.
claims.source: Strikingly, old EE progenitors had increased expression of deadpan (dpn) and other pro-neural genes (Figure 2F), the upregulation of which was recently described as a hallmark of neuroendocrine tumor stem cells in the midgut (Li et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: A general upregulation of neural stem cell (NSC) markers was noted in bulk RNA-seq.
claims.source: We also noted a general upregulation of these neural stem cell (NSC) markers in our bulk RNA-seq (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The upregulation of EE genes in aged ISCs observed by bulk RNA-seq was driven by an increase in the number of EE-specified ISCs.
claims.source: Critically, our scRNA-seq data revealed that the upregulation of EE genes in aged ISCs observed by bulk RNA-seq was driven by an increase in the number of EE-specified ISCs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the scRNA-seq data showing increased EE progenitor cells.

claims.claim: Both methods (genetic reporter and immunostaining) showed a significant and progressive increase in the proportion of EE cells as the animal ages.
claims.source: Both methods showed a significant and progressive increase in the proportion of EE cells as the animal ages (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: An increase in esg and Pros double-positive cells in old midguts was observed, indicating an increase in EE progenitor cells.
claims.source: We also observed an increase in esg and Pros double-positive cells in old midguts (Figure 3B), indicating an increase in EE progenitor cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Luminex xMAP technology revealed a 153% increase in H3K27me2 as well as a 65% increase in pan-acetylated H3 in old flies.
claims.source: This analysis revealed a 153% increase in H3K27me2 as well as a 65% increase in pan-acetylated H3 in old flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Luminex xMAP data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: ISC nuclei exhibited a lower intensity of H3K27me2 than EEs in young animals.
claims.source: Antibody staining for H3K27me2 confirmed that H3K27me2 levels change in older intestines, albeit in a cell-type-specific manner: ISC nuclei exhibited a lower intensity of H3K27me2 than EEs in young animals (Figure 4A)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: ISCs in old midguts exhibited a significant increase in H3K27me2 intensity, approaching EE levels.
claims.source: however, ISCs in old midguts exhibited a significant increase in H3K27me2 intensity, approaching EE levels (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Loss of E(z) or Pc significantly reduced the proportion of lineages containing Pros+ EE cells.
claims.source: Remarkably, loss of E(z) or Pc significantly reduced the proportion of lineages containing Pros+ EE cells (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by clonal analysis data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: A decrease in H3K27me2 intensity was observed upon E(z) knockdown.
claims.source: Additionally, we observed a decrease in H3K27me2 intensity upon E(z) knockdown (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Ecc15-induced ISC proliferation was not affected by Pc or E(z) knockdown.
claims.source: Ecc15-induced ISC proliferation was not affected by Pc or E(z) knockdown, indicating that PRC only influences specification of ISCs and their daughter cells without impacting proliferative capacity of ISCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Knockdown of trx resulted in increased numbers of Pros+ cells, as well as in larger GFP+ cell lineages.
claims.source: Using esg-F/Ots, knockdown of trx resulted in increased numbers of Pros+ cells, as well as in larger GFP+ cell lineages, indicating that loss of trx promotes both ISC proliferation and EE specification (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by clonal analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Heterozygous trxE2 mutant flies exhibited increased Pros+ cell numbers as well as increased ISC proliferation.
claims.source: Similarly, heterozygous trxE2 mutant flies exhibited increased Pros+ cell numbers as well as increased ISC proliferation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and proliferation assay data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Knocking down trx in esg+ cells only also resulted in increased proliferation.
claims.source: while knocking down trx in esg+ cells only also resulted in increased proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: GSEA revealed a positive enrichment for GO terms involving ribosome biology and protein production after Pc knockdown.
claims.source: GSEA revealed a positive enrichment for GO terms involving ribosome biology and protein production after Pc knockdown (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Knocking down Pc in ISCs significantly decreased expression of several EE genes, including ase and Synaptotagmin 4 (Syt4).
claims.source: Notably, knocking down Pc in ISCs significantly decreased expression of several EE genes, including ase and Synaptotagmin 4 (Syt4), and resulted in lower expression of key specification genes scute (sc) and phyllopod (phyl) (Figure 5A,C, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: An increase in expression (albeit not significant) of EC genes was noted after Pc knockdown.
claims.source: We also noted an increase in expression (albeit not significant) of EC genes (often encoding proteins involved in proteolysis, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Pc normally represses EC genes in ISCs and is required for EE gene expression.
claims.source: This suggests that Pc normally represses EC genes in ISCs and is required for EE gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data after Pc knockdown.

claims.claim: Knockdown of trx resulted in a significant upregulation of many EE genes and cell cycle genes.
claims.source: Conversely, knockdown of trx resulted in a significant upregulation of many EE genes and cell cycle genes (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 5), consistent with the proposed antagonistic functions of trx and Pc on ISC lineage specification described above (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: GSEA revealed a positive enrichment in GO terms involving neuron differentiation, plasma membrane localization, and peptide hormone secretion after trx knockdown.
claims.source: Furthermore, GSEA revealed a positive enrichment in GO terms involving neuron differentiation, plasma membrane localization, and peptide hormone secretion, all of which suggest EE cell fate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: sc overexpression rescued the EE differentiation deficiency after Pc loss.
claims.source: Notably, sc overexpression rescued the EE differentiation deficiency after Pc loss (Figure 5D) indicating that it acts downstream of the Pc complex in regulating EE differentiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments shown in the figure.

claims.claim: sc acts downstream of the Pc complex in regulating EE differentiation.
claims.source: Notably, sc overexpression rescued the EE differentiation deficiency after Pc loss (Figure 5D) indicating that it acts downstream of the Pc complex in regulating EE differentiation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction experiments.

claims.claim: Pc1 heterozygous mutants exhibited normal levels of EEs.
claims.source: Pc1 heterozygous mutants exhibited normal levels of EEs (Figure 5E)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: trxE2 heterozygotes had higher EE levels.
claims.source: while trxE2 heterozygotes had higher EE levels as shown before (Figure 4C, Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Re-balancing Pc and trx transcript levels restored EE numbers back to wild-type proportions.
claims.source: Strikingly, re-balancing Pc and trx transcript levels restored EE numbers back to wild-type proportions, thus highlighting the importance of maintaining stable stoichiometry between these factors in EE differentiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from trans-heterozygous mutants.

claims.claim: Knocking down Pc in ISCs resulted in a moderate decrease in global chromatin accessibility.
claims.source: Intriguingly, though PRC is traditionally thought to maintain a repressive chromatin state, knocking down Pc in ISCs resulted in a moderate decrease in global chromatin accessibility (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Regions that were most differentially regulated after Pc knockdown were intergenic and intronic regions.
claims.source: Regions that were most differentially regulated were intergenic and intronic regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Differential peak analysis on promoter regions revealed a decrease in accessibility of ISC genes such as esg and spdo as well as the pro-neural gene dpn after Pc knockdown.
claims.source: Differential peak analysis on promoter regions (20% of total differential peaks, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B) revealed a decrease in accessibility of ISC genes such as esg and spdo as well as the pro-neural gene dpn (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Promoters with increased accessibility after Pc knockdown included homeobox transcription factors Abd-B and Lim1, as well as chinmo.
claims.source: Promoters with increased accessibility included homeobox transcription factors Abd-B and Lim1, as well as a chinmo, a BTB-zinc finger transcription factor involved in regulating stem cell self-renewal (Dillard et al., 2018; Flaherty et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data.

claims.claim: Promoters of Lim1 and chinmo were also differentially accessible in aging ISCs and their transcripts were differentially regulated.
claims.source: Promoters of Lim1 and chinmo were also differentially accessible in aging ISCs and their transcripts were differentially regulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: EE gene promoters were not significantly affected after Pc-RNAi, suggesting their expression may be regulated independently of promoter accessibility.
claims.source: Interestingly, EE gene promoters were not significantly affected after Pc-RNAi, suggesting their expression may be regulated independently of promoter accessibility.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the ATAC-seq data after Pc knockdown.

claims.claim: The progressive increase in the proportion of Pros+ EE cells and of esg+/Pros+ EE progenitor cells observed in aging control animals was significantly reduced after Pc knock-down.
claims.source: Strikingly, the progressive increase in the proportion of Pros+ EE cells and of esg+/Pros+ EE progenitor cells observed in aging control animals was significantly reduced after Pc knock-down (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The decrease in Pros+ cells after Pc knockdown was not due to a loss of ISCs.
claims.source: The decrease in Pros+ cells was not due to a loss of ISCs, as ISC numbers were not changed at either the young or old time-points, suggesting Pc is mainly required for EE specification, but does not affect ISC viability (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Long-term Pc knock-down reduced levels of dysplasia in aged animals.
claims.source: Importantly, long-term Pc knock-down also reduced levels of dysplasia in aged animals (Figure 6A), suggesting that the increase in EE cells contributes to age-related intestinal dysplasia.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dysplasia scoring data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The increase in EE cells contributes to age-related intestinal dysplasia.
claims.source: Importantly, long-term Pc knock-down also reduced levels of dysplasia in aged animals (Figure 6A), suggesting that the increase in EE cells contributes to age-related intestinal dysplasia.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the dysplasia scoring data after Pc knockdown.

claims.claim: Dysplasia levels correlated with the percentage of EE progenitors regardless of age.
claims.source: In fact, dysplasia levels (categorized based on GFP+ cell number, distribution and morphology; Biteau et al., 2010) correlated with the percentage of EE progenitors regardless of age (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The proportion of EEs and EE progenitors increased in conventionally aged flies.
claims.source: Indeed, while the proportion of EEs and EE progenitors increased in conventionally aged flies, these increases were significantly reduced in axenically aged flies (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The increases in EE and EE progenitor proportions were significantly reduced in axenically aged flies.
claims.source: Indeed, while the proportion of EEs and EE progenitors increased in conventionally aged flies, these increases were significantly reduced in axenically aged flies (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Knocking down the negative regulator of JNK, puckered (puc), in the ISC lineage or in ISCs specifically resulted in a significant increase in the proportion of Pros+ EE cells after 4 days of over-expression.
claims.source: Knocking down the negative regulator of JNK, puckered (puc), in the ISC lineage (using the esg-F/Ots system) or in ISCs specifically (ISCts), resulted in a significant increase in the proportion of Pros+ EE cells after 4 days of over-expression (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Age-related inflammation and stress signaling, particularly activation of the JNK pathway in ISCs, influences ISC lineage choice towards the EE fate.
claims.source: These results support a role for age-related inflammation and stress signaling, particularly activation of the JNK pathway in ISCs, in influencing ISC lineage choice towards the EE fate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the puc knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Loss of lineage fidelity in ISCs of aging flies results in an imbalance of EE vs EC differentiation and contributes to epithelial dysplasia.
claims.source: Our study identifies a loss of lineage fidelity in ISCs of aging flies that results in an imbalance of EE vs EC differentiation and contributes to epithelial dysplasia.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in the study.

claims.claim: This loss of lineage fidelity is caused by age-related deregulation of Pc function in ISCs, resulting in de-repression and preferential expression of EE genes.
claims.source: This loss of lineage fidelity is caused by age-related deregulation of Pc function in ISCs, resulting in de-repression and preferential expression of EE genes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The chronic activation of stress signaling in ISCs, triggered by local and systemic inflammatory stimuli in the aging intestine, promotes the deregulation of Pc-controlled gene activity.
claims.source: We propose that the chronic activation of stress signaling in ISCs, triggered by local and systemic inflammatory stimuli in the aging intestine, promotes the deregulation of Pc-controlled gene activity (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Genetically elevating JNK activity in ISCs disrupts lineage fidelity and causes an increase in the proportion of EEs in the gut epithelium.
claims.source: This is supported by the fact that genetically elevating JNK activity in ISCs disrupts lineage fidelity and causes an increase in the proportion of EEs in the gut epithelium.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the puc knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: The increase in EE numbers contributes to epithelial dysplasia in the aging gut, as EEs can promote ISC proliferation.
claims.source: The increase in EE numbers contributes to epithelial dysplasia in the aging gut, as EEs can promote ISC proliferation (Amcheslavsky et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the dysplasia data and a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The stress-induced changes in lineage fidelity in ISCs likely set up a vicious cycle that causes progressive dysplasia and results in disruption of epithelial structure and function in the aging intestine.
claims.source: The stress-induced changes in lineage fidelity in ISCs thus likely set up a vicious cycle that causes progressive dysplasia and results in disruption of epithelial structure and function in the aging intestine.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The scRNA-seq analysis of the Drosophila gut is consistent with a recent scRNA-seq study from young flies.
claims.source: Our scRNA-seq analysis of the Drosophila gut is consistent with a recent scRNA-seq study from young flies (Hung et al., 2020), but also captures the changes in intestinal cell states across aging.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with a previous study.

claims.claim: The transcriptional signature distinguishing the 'stressed ISC' population encompasses over 25% of significantly upregulated genes observed in bulk RNA-seq study from purified old ISCs.
claims.source: The transcriptional signature distinguishing this cell population encompasses over 25% of significantly upregulated genes observed in our bulk RNA-seq study from purified old ISCs, supporting the robustness and complementarity of the two methods.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The appearance of the 'stressed' stem cell population is consistent with the previously described increase in inflammatory and oxidative stress in the aging intestinal epithelium.
claims.source: The appearance of this 'stressed' stem cell population is further consistent with the previously described increase in inflammatory and oxidative stress in the aging intestinal epithelium, and may reflect the age-associated accumulation of oxidative, proteostatic and genomic damage in these cells (Buchon et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014; Hochmuth et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012; Rodriguez-Fernandez et al., 2019; Siudeja et al., 2015; Sousa-Victor et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The majority of old ISCs reside in an activated cell state (~50%), whereas the 'stressed ISC' population makes up only a small percentage (<10%).
claims.source: Overall, the majority of old ISCs reside in an activated cell state (~50%), whereas the 'stressed ISC' population makes up only a small percentage (<10%).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The 'stressed' ISC population may represent a correlate to mammalian senescent cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the p53 and DNA repair pathways are upregulated in this cell population, while cell cycle genes are repressed, indicating that these cells may represent a correlate to mammalian senescent cells.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the gene expression profile of the 'stressed' ISC population.

claims.claim: In a neuroendocrine tumor model, ISCs undergo an identity switch that results in the acquisition of NSC-like features.
claims.source: It was recently shown that in a neuroendocrine tumor model, ISCs undergo an identity switch that results in the acquisition of NSC-like features (Li et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The NSC gene signature was also upregulated in old ISCs analyzed by bulk RNAseq.
claims.source: This NSC gene signature was also upregulated in old ISCs analyzed by bulk RNAseq, suggesting that a general upregulation of these genes may contribute to age-related ISC phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: ATAC-seq data from purified ISC populations revealed only moderate changes in chromatin organization in ISCs of increasingly older animals.
claims.source: Our ATAC-seq data from purified ISC populations revealed only moderate changes in chromatin organization in ISCs of increasingly older animals, suggesting that ISC gene regulation is tightly controlled throughout life.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data.

claims.claim: The significant increase in H3K27 dimethylation levels in aging ISCs supports a role for increases in H3K27me2 in skewing ISC identity towards the EE fate.
claims.source: At the same time, the significant increase in H3K27 dimethylation levels in aging ISCs, the fact that H3K27me2 levels are higher in EEs than in ISCs in young guts, and the observation that E(z)-mediated methylation of H3K27 is required for EE specification, all support a role for increases in H3K27me2 in skewing ISC identity towards the EE fate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the H3K27me2 data and the genetic experiments.

claims.claim: The broad genomic distribution of H3K27me2 was shown to suppress aberrant gene activation by controlling enhancer fidelity in mammals.
claims.source: The broad genomic distribution of H3K27me2 was shown to suppress aberrant gene activation by controlling enhancer fidelity in mammals (Ferrari et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: H3K27me2 controls access to transcription factors and RNA Pol II to DNA in flies.
claims.source: and access to transcription factors and RNA Pol II to DNA in flies (Lee et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Perturbing the ratio of H3K27me2/H3K27me3 in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) affected the acquisition and repression of specific fates of these cells.
claims.source: One study found that perturbing the ratio of H3K27me2/H3K27me3 in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) affected the acquisition and repression of specific fates of these cells (Juan et al., 2016), indicating the importance of appropriate regulation of these marks in different cell types.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The expression of Pc, E(z) and other PcG genes, as well as the expression of trx, Trl and z, was not significantly altered in aging ISCs.
claims.source: Of note, the expression of Pc, E(z) and other PcG genes, as well as the expression of trx, Trl and z, was not significantly altered in aging ISCs, suggesting that aging most likely affects their post-transcriptional regulation and/or function.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Aging most likely affects the post-transcriptional regulation and/or function of PcG and TrxG proteins.
claims.source: Of note, the expression of Pc, E(z) and other PcG genes, as well as the expression of trx, Trl and z, was not significantly altered in aging ISCs, suggesting that aging most likely affects their post-transcriptional regulation and/or function.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: In aging HSCs and muscle SCs, the H3K27me3 signal exhibits broader coverage and increased intensity at transcriptional start sites and intergenic regions.
claims.source: Age-related changes in H3K27 methylation have been reported in mammalian SC populations: in aging HSCs and muscle SCs, the H3K27me3 signal exhibits broader coverage and increased intensity at transcriptional start sites and intergenic regions (Liu et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: There is an evolutionarily conserved effect of aging on PRC function in tissue stem cells.

results.result: ATAC-seq analysis of aging ISCs reveals overall stable chromatin accessibility with differential accessibility at Polycomb target gene promoters. Motif analysis identified enrichment for Trithorax-like (Trl) and Zeste (z) motifs in differentially accessible promoter regions across aging time-points, suggesting potential mis-regulation of PcG proteins in old ISCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C36-C45 are supported by ATAC-seq data showing stable global chromatin accessibility (C36-C39) but differential accessibility at specific promoter regions (C40-C42) enriched for Trl and z motifs (C43-C44). The inference that this suggests PcG mis-regulation (C45) is reasonable given the known function of Trl and z in recruiting PcG proteins (C44). The data quality appears robust with appropriate replication and correlation analyses.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis reveals progressive transcriptional changes in aging ISCs with significant enrichment of enteroendocrine (EE) cell specification genes. Young ISCs cluster separately from mid-aged to geriatric ISCs, with increasing numbers of differentially expressed genes at old and geriatric time-points. GSEA shows consistent enrichment of EE genes in upregulated genes during aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C46-C56 are supported by RNA-seq data showing progressive transcriptional changes (C49-C52), enrichment of EE genes (C54-C55), and appropriate statistical analyses including Pearson correlation and PCA (C49-C50). The correlation between chromatin accessibility and gene expression changes is appropriately assessed (C46-C48). Sample sizes and statistical methods appear adequate with adjusted p-values reported.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq identifies age-specific cell states in the Drosophila midgut, including 'stressed ISC' and 'damaged cell' populations that are almost exclusively present in old flies. These populations show enrichment for stress response genes, DNA repair pathways, and are consistent with previously reported elevated stress signaling and DNA damage in the aged epithelium.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C69 are supported by scRNA-seq data showing distinct cell clusters (C58-C60), appropriate batch correction, and gene set enrichment analyses (C61, C64, C66). The characterization of 'stressed' and 'damaged' cell states is supported by GO and pathway analyses (C64, C66). The consistency with prior work (C67-C69) strengthens the interpretation. The pseudo-bulk analysis validates findings against bulk RNA-seq (C62-C63).

results.result: Trajectory analysis of EE progenitor cells reveals a significant increase in EE progenitor cell numbers in old samples, with increased expression of pro-neural genes including deadpan (dpn). The upregulation of EE genes in aged ISCs observed by bulk RNA-seq is driven by an increase in the number of EE-specified ISCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by trajectory analysis of scRNA-seq data (C70), quantification showing increased EE progenitor cells (C71), and expression analysis of pro-neural genes (C72-C73). The integration of bulk and single-cell RNA-seq data (C74) provides strong support for the conclusion that increased EE gene expression reflects increased EE-specified ISC numbers rather than per-cell expression changes.

results.result: Immunohistochemistry confirms a progressive increase in the proportion of EE cells and EE progenitor cells with age in the Drosophila intestine.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by immunohistochemistry data using both genetic reporters and direct immunostaining (C75), with appropriate quantification and statistical analysis. The data validate the scRNA-seq findings using an orthogonal method. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=6-10 per group) with multiple independent experiments.

results.result: Aging ISCs accumulate H3K27me2, approaching levels observed in EE cells. Luminex xMAP analysis shows a 153% increase in H3K27me2 in old flies, and immunostaining confirms cell-type-specific increases in ISCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are supported by two independent methods: Luminex xMAP technology for quantitative measurement (C77) and immunohistochemistry for cell-type-specific analysis (C78-C79). The convergence of these methods strengthens the conclusion. Statistical significance is reported with appropriate sample sizes. The observation that ISCs acquire EE-like H3K27me2 levels supports the lineage fidelity hypothesis.

results.result: Loss of E(z) or Pc significantly reduces EE cell differentiation in ISC lineages without affecting ISC proliferative capacity. E(z) knockdown decreases H3K27me2 intensity.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by clonal analysis showing reduced EE differentiation (C80), immunostaining confirming decreased H3K27me2 (C81), and proliferation assays showing no effect on ISC proliferation (C82). The use of two independent RNAi lines for each gene strengthens the conclusions. Statistical analyses show significance with appropriate controls.

results.result: Loss of trithorax (trx) increases both EE cell numbers and ISC proliferation, demonstrating antagonistic functions of trx and Pc in ISC lineage specification.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by multiple genetic approaches: RNAi knockdown (C83, C85) and heterozygous mutant analysis (C84). The data show consistent increases in both EE differentiation and proliferation across different experimental systems. Statistical significance is demonstrated with appropriate controls. The antagonistic relationship with Pc is well-supported.

results.result: Pc knockdown in ISCs decreases expression of EE specification genes (ase, Syt4, sc, phyl) and increases EC gene expression, suggesting Pc normally represses EC genes and is required for EE gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are supported by RNA-seq data after Pc knockdown showing decreased EE gene expression (C87) and increased EC gene expression (C88). GSEA analysis supports the functional interpretation (C86). The inference that Pc represses EC genes and promotes EE gene expression (C89) is reasonable given the data, though the EC gene increase is noted as not statistically significant (C88), which appropriately tempers the conclusion.

results.result: Trithorax (trx) knockdown results in significant upregulation of EE genes and cell cycle genes, with GSEA showing enrichment for neuron differentiation and EE cell fate-related GO terms.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by RNA-seq data showing upregulation of EE and cell cycle genes (C90) and GSEA analysis confirming enrichment of EE-related pathways (C91). The data are consistent with the antagonistic relationship between trx and Pc observed in the phenotypic analyses. Statistical significance is appropriately reported.

results.result: Overexpression of scute (sc) rescues EE differentiation deficiency after Pc loss, indicating sc acts downstream of the Pc complex in regulating EE differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by genetic interaction experiments showing rescue of the Pc knockdown phenotype by sc overexpression (C92). The epistasis analysis appropriately supports the conclusion that sc acts downstream of Pc (C93). Statistical analysis shows significance with appropriate controls. This provides mechanistic insight into the Pc-mediated regulation of EE differentiation.

results.result: Re-balancing Pc and trx transcript levels in trans-heterozygous mutants restores EE numbers to wild-type proportions, highlighting the importance of maintaining stable stoichiometry between these factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 are supported by genetic analysis of single and trans-heterozygous mutants showing that Pc1 heterozygotes have normal EE levels (C94), trxE2 heterozygotes have elevated EE levels (C95), and the double heterozygote restores normal levels (C96). This elegant genetic experiment demonstrates the importance of Pc/trx balance. Statistical analysis is appropriate with adequate sample sizes.

results.result: Pc knockdown results in moderate decrease in global chromatin accessibility, with differential accessibility primarily in intergenic and intronic regions. Promoter analysis reveals decreased accessibility at ISC genes (esg, spdo, dpn) and increased accessibility at transcription factor genes (Abd-B, Lim1, chinmo).
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 are supported by ATAC-seq data after Pc knockdown showing global and region-specific changes in chromatin accessibility (C97-C101). The observation that EE gene promoters are not significantly affected (C102) is appropriately noted and suggests indirect regulation. The data provide mechanistic insight into Pc function, though the unexpected decrease in global accessibility (C97) warrants further investigation.

results.result: Long-term Pc knockdown in ISCs prevents the age-related increase in EE cells and EE progenitors and reduces dysplasia in aged animals, suggesting increased EE cells contribute to age-related intestinal dysplasia.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 are supported by long-term (28 day) Pc knockdown experiments showing reduced EE cell accumulation (C103), maintained ISC numbers (C104), reduced dysplasia (C105), and correlation between EE progenitor numbers and dysplasia levels (C107). The inference that increased EE cells contribute to dysplasia (C106) is well-supported by the correlation and rescue data. This demonstrates the functional significance of the age-related changes in lineage fidelity.

results.result: Axenic aging significantly reduces the age-related increase in EE cells and EE progenitors compared to conventional aging, suggesting commensal dysbiosis contributes to the shift in ISC lineage fidelity.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 are supported by comparison of conventionally and axenically aged flies showing reduced EE cell accumulation in the absence of microbiota (C109). Appropriate controls and statistical analyses are included. This links the age-related changes in lineage fidelity to environmental factors (commensal dysbiosis) and suggests a mechanism involving inflammation.

results.result: JNK pathway activation in ISCs (via puckered knockdown) increases the proportion of EE cells, supporting a role for age-related inflammation and stress signaling in influencing ISC lineage choice toward the EE fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 are supported by genetic manipulation of JNK signaling showing increased EE differentiation after puc knockdown (C110). The use of two different driver systems (esg-F/Ots and ISCts) strengthens the conclusion. The inference that age-related inflammation influences lineage choice (C111) is well-supported by integration with the axenic aging data. This provides a mechanistic link between environmental stress and lineage fidelity.

results.result: The study proposes a model where age-related deregulation of Pc function in ISCs, driven by chronic stress signaling and inflammation, causes loss of lineage fidelity resulting in increased EE differentiation that contributes to epithelial dysplasia through a vicious cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 represent the integrated model of the study. The model is well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: ATAC-seq and RNA-seq showing Pc target deregulation (C2-C3), scRNA-seq showing increased EE progenitors (C71), immunohistochemistry confirming increased EE cells (C75), genetic experiments demonstrating Pc requirement (C80), rescue experiments preventing dysplasia (C105), axenic aging reducing EE accumulation (C109), and JNK activation promoting EE fate (C110). The proposed vicious cycle (C117) is a reasonable inference though speculative.

results.result: The scRNA-seq analysis identifies a 'stressed ISC' population that increases with age, is consistent with previous studies, and may represent a correlate to mammalian senescent cells based on gene expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 are supported by scRNA-seq data showing consistency with prior work (C118), overlap with bulk RNA-seq (C119), and appropriate characterization of the stressed ISC population (C120-C121). The speculation that this population may represent senescent cells (C122) is appropriately tentative and based on gene expression patterns (p53, DNA repair pathways upregulated; cell cycle genes repressed). This represents a valuable characterization of age-related ISC states.

results.result: Neural stem cell (NSC) gene signatures are upregulated in old ISCs, similar to a neuroendocrine tumor model, suggesting this may contribute to age-related ISC phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 are supported by comparison with a previous tumor model study (C123) and bulk RNA-seq data showing NSC gene upregulation (C124). The functional significance of this observation remains unclear and requires further investigation. This represents an interesting observation that may warrant follow-up studies.

results.result: ATAC-seq reveals moderate changes in chromatin organization in aging ISCs, but the significant increase in H3K27me2 levels supports a role for this modification in skewing ISC identity toward the EE fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 are supported by ATAC-seq data showing overall stability (C125) and H3K27me2 quantification showing increases in aging ISCs (C77-C79). The inference that H3K27me2 increases contribute to EE fate specification (C126) is supported by the observation that EEs have higher H3K27me2 than ISCs in young guts and that E(z) is required for EE specification. This provides mechanistic insight into the epigenetic basis of lineage fidelity changes.

results.result: The expression of Pc, E(z), and other PcG genes is not significantly altered in aging ISCs, suggesting aging affects their post-transcriptional regulation and/or function rather than expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 are supported by RNA-seq data showing no significant changes in PcG gene expression (C130). The inference that aging affects post-transcriptional regulation or function (C131) is reasonable given the observed changes in H3K27me2 levels and chromatin accessibility at Pc target genes. This is an important observation that focuses attention on regulatory mechanisms beyond transcription.

results.result: Pc activity regulates multiple aspects of ISC specification, with loss of Pc inducing EC gene expression, repressing EE gene expression, and decreasing chromatin accessibility at ISC identity genes, while ISC function remains largely intact.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C137 are supported by integration of RNA-seq (C87-C88), ATAC-seq (C99), and functional assays (C82, C104, C136) after Pc knockdown. The conclusion that Pc primarily regulates lineage commitment rather than ISC viability or proliferation (C137) is well-supported by the data. This provides a comprehensive view of Pc function in ISCs.

results.result: The antagonistic function of trx in EE differentiation is consistent with known trx-Pc antagonism, and trx loss also induces cell cycle genes and ISC proliferation, consistent with recent studies on TrxG factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 are supported by the trx knockdown data (C83-C85, C90) and consistency with prior work (C138, C140). The observation that trx affects both differentiation and proliferation (C139) suggests broader roles in ISC function. The consistency with recent studies (C140) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: The interaction between JNK and Pc in the ISC lineage is complex, with JNK activation promoting EE specification while Pc knockdown inhibits EE specification, contrasting with previous reports of JNK suppressing Pc function.
results.evaluation: Claim C150 is supported by the data showing opposite effects of JNK activation (C110) and Pc knockdown (C80) on EE specification. The observation that this differs from previous reports (C149) is appropriately noted. This suggests context-dependent interactions between JNK and Pc that warrant further mechanistic investigation. The apparent paradox is acknowledged but not fully resolved.

results.result: The study concludes that altered ISC cell states in old flies affect intestinal homeostasis and contribute to dysplasia, with age-associated deregulation of lineage fidelity due to elevated stress and Pc misregulation as key drivers. Pc group proteins are proposed as potential therapeutic targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C163 represent well-supported summary conclusions based on the integrated data from the study. The proposal that Pc group proteins may represent therapeutic targets (C164) is appropriately speculative and based on the demonstrated functional importance of Pc in maintaining lineage fidelity and preventing dysplasia. This represents a reasonable extrapolation from the findings.

results.result: The introduction establishes the biological context by reviewing established knowledge about stem cell lineage fidelity, epigenetic regulation, Polycomb and Trithorax group proteins, and the Drosophila intestinal stem cell system.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C33 represent background knowledge and citations to previous work that establish the context for the study. These claims are appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature and reflect established knowledge in the field. They provide necessary background but do not represent novel findings of this study.

results.result: The experimental design uses FACS-purified ISCs from flies across their lifespan, with ISCs specifically labeled using the esg-Gal4, UAS-2xYFP; Su(H)-Gal80 system.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 describe the experimental design and genetic labeling system used to isolate ISCs. The approach is well-established and appropriate for the study. The use of Su(H)-Gal80 to restrict expression to ISCs (excluding EBs) is a validated method. This represents sound experimental design.

results.result: Previous studies have shown that H3K27me2 regulates enhancer fidelity and transcription factor access in mammals and flies, and that age-related changes in H3K27 methylation occur in mammalian stem cells, suggesting evolutionarily conserved effects of aging on PRC function.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129, C132-C133 cite previous work on H3K27me2 function and age-related changes in H3K27 methylation. These claims appropriately contextualize the current findings within the broader literature and support the evolutionary conservation of the mechanisms identified. The inference of evolutionary conservation (C133) is reasonable given the cited evidence.

results.result: Previous studies in the mouse intestine have shown that PRC1 and PRC2 regulate ISC identity and lineage specification, with some discrepancies regarding PRC2's role under homeostatic conditions. Age-related changes in the mammalian intestine include increased secretory cell lineage.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C148 cite previous work on PRC function in the mammalian intestine and age-related changes. These claims appropriately contextualize the current findings and note discrepancies in the literature (C144-C145) that have been reconciled by more recent work (C146). This provides important comparative context for interpreting the Drosophila findings.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes the findings within the broader literature on intestinal inflammation, EE cell function in disease, and PRC2 function in cancer, noting that Pc group proteins may represent therapeutic targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C160 cite relevant literature on inflammation, EE cells in disease, and PRC2 in cancer to contextualize the findings. The discussion appropriately connects the Drosophila findings to mammalian biology and disease. The experimental demonstration that lowering EE numbers reduces dysplasia (C155) provides direct support for a pathological role of increased EE cells.
